extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, law students, and legal scholars studying remedies in patent infringement suits
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and principles for computing and awarding an infringer's profits in equity in patent-infringement litigation, including what counts as profit, allowable credits, apportionment between patented and non-patented features, and procedural mechanics for taking an account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits in equity defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits in equity include all those pecuniary benefits which the defendant has derived from the infringement and are regarded in equity as the property of the owner of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains equitable theory: defendant ordered to render an account and pay sum ascertained; enforced by usual equity measures. (See introductory §1138 and case citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant must render an account; master follows fixed rules
rubrics_metrics.description: To ascertain and compel payment the defendant is ordered to render an account; the account is taken before a master who reports the value of profits and is bound by certain rules about items charged, credited, and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Master's duties include investigation and estimate of net amount; cannot depart from rules governing items and evidence. (Referenced throughout discussion of §§1156–1157 and cases cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Two principal classes of infringement (use vs sale) govern the account
rubrics_metrics.description: All cases of infringement may be divided into (1) unlawful use, or making and use of the patented invention, and (2) unlawful sale, or manufacture and sale of the patented invention; the items in the account differ for each class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise treats sale/manufacture-and-sale first because rules are fewer; classification determines what receipts and credits are relevant. (See §1138–1139 discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits on sale mode are only those actually received on articles sold and paid for
rubrics_metrics.description: Where infringement consists in sale or manufacture and sale, pecuniary benefits are the profits actually received by the defendant upon the patented articles which he has sold; articles made and not sold, sold but unpaid, or sold at price not exceeding cost yield no profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites cases (Tilghman v. Proctor, Burdett v. Estey, Elizabeth v. Pavement Co.). Emphasizes that only profits actually realized and paid for are object of inquiry; unsold/inventory cannot be charged as profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure of profit for sold articles: price obtained minus cost of making and selling
rubrics_metrics.description: For each article sold in violation of the patent, profit is measured by the difference between the cost of making and selling and the price obtained; defendant charged with amounts received and credited with manufacturing/marketing costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where uncomplicated, main difficulty is which credits to allow. Several cases cited illustrating application (Burdett v. Estey, Rubber Co. v. Goodyear, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable credits: cost of manufacture (materials, labor)
rubrics_metrics.description: The defendant must be credited with the cost of manufacture, including the price paid for materials and labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Gould's Mfg. Co. v. Cowing, Buerk v. Imhaeuser, Rubber Co. v. Goodyear. Cost of making the articles must be allowed to determine net profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable credits: interest on actually expended capital for machinery/power, value of use of tools, loss by waste
rubrics_metrics.description: Allow interest on amount actually expended for machinery and power; allow value of use of tools; allow loss occasioned by waste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If interest or expense was actually incurred it should be allowed; if not incurred, not to be deducted. Cases: Troy Iron & Nail Factory v. Coming; Gould's Mfg. Co. v. Cowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable credits: rental of buildings and reasonable salaries of superintendents and higher employees
rubrics_metrics.description: The rental of buildings necessarily occupied in the manufacture and reasonable salaries of superintendents or other higher employees are part of manufacturing cost and are to be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Steam Stone Cutter Co. v. Windsor Mfg. Co.; American Nicholson Pavement Co. v. City of Elizabeth. Distinguishes reasonable salaries (allowed) from extraordinary salaries (disallowed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable credits: royalties paid for machinery/processes and ordinary running/marketing expenses
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasonable royalties paid upon machinery or processes used in production, ordinary running expenses, and cost of marketing (freight, storage, commissions, warehouse/shop rental, clerks' salaries, collection expenses) should be allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases cited include Gould's Mfg. Co. v. Cowing, Zane v. Peck Brothers, and others. When defendant in general business, apportionment rules apply (see separate entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowable credit for decrease in cost from defendant's own improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant has cheapened the cost of producing the infringing device by an improvement of his own, he is entitled to a corresponding credit in ascertaining profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Mason v. Graham. Defendant must prove such improvements affirmatively to obtain the credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disallowed credits: time and services of the infringer and interest on capital stock
rubrics_metrics.description: The time and services of the defendant (or, for corporations, of its stockholders unless bona fide employees) and interest on capital invested in the general business cannot be credited against profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains equity policy: infringers cannot shield gains by treating them as salaries; interest on capital stock generally disallowed (Rubber Co. v. Goodyear; contra Wilbur v. Beecher).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disallowed credits: insurance and similar items that are not chargeable to plaintiff
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurance on the property employed and similar items are not to be credited as deductions from profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mentioned alongside interest and services as disallowed; references to cases addressing property-related costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment of general business expenses when infringing article is one department
rubrics_metrics.description: When defendant is engaged in a general business and the patented invention constitutes only one department of sales, general business expenses must be apportioned in the ratio of sales of infringing to non-infringing articles, and the proportion of the former charged as expenses of their sale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides method: ascertain gross proceeds of each class, deduct special/peculiar expenses pro forma, then allot proportionate share of general expenses to each. Examples and cases: Gould's Mfg. Co. v. Cowing; Hitchcock v. Tremaine.

rubrics_metrics.name: No deduction for losses on unsold or cost-priced infringing articles
rubrics_metrics.description: No allowance can be made for losses on infringing articles which have been sold at cost or less than cost, or which have not been paid for or remain unsold; profits only arise on articles sold at a profit and paid for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains rationale that inventor should not bear infringer's business losses; cites cases including discussion of unsold inventory and unpaid sales.

rubrics_metrics.name: When infringing article contains additional (non-patented) marketable features, apportion price and cost
rubrics_metrics.description: If the infringing article contains substantial non-patented features that contribute to market value, the price and cost must be separated so that the deduction of the latter from the former indicates the profit due to the patented invention; deduct the value attributable to other matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives method: price for patented invention = price for whole article less what it would have brought without the invention; cost is difference in expense with and without invention. Cases: Maier v. Brown; Fay v. Allen; Roemer v. Simon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recovery limited to profits properly apportioned to patented feature when patent covers part only
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee limited to recovery of profits that can be properly apportioned to use of his improvement; where patent covers only a part of an article, recovery is confined to profits attributable to the patented feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Seymour v. McCormick, Mowry v. Whitney, Littlefield v. Perry. Emphasizes need for proof and that inability to separate may limit recovery to nominal damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: If plaintiff cannot prove apportionment, only nominal damages may be awarded
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee is unable to prove how much of the entire profit upon the machine is due to his patent, he can recover only nominal damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Blake v. Robertson and discussion in Maier v. Brown: equity will not award speculative sums beyond proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer's profit may be allowed depending on mode of infringement and evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The manufacturer's profit enters differently: where infringement is by making and selling the patented article, the manufacturer's profit enters the profit resulting from the sale; where infringement is use-only, manufacturer's profit is not a direct allowable item unless evidence shows it is attributable to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise notes dispute in authority; cites Simpson v. Davis, Buerk v. Imhaeuser, and Rubber Co. v. Goodyear. Consider whether patent increases advantage relative to defendant's prior alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissions and agent payments treated as profits to the payee, not principal
rubrics_metrics.description: A commission paid to an agent is a profit to be accounted for by the agent (not by principal); commissions claimed but not actually paid cannot be allowed as credits by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Steiger v. Heidelberger and Piper v. Brown. Distinguishes agency payments and when they may be considered in accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money paid to protect defendant's vendees or guaranties of title not deductible
rubrics_metrics.description: Money paid by defendant to protect his vendees from the plaintiff or guaranties of title given to purchasers are not allowed in the account of profits; such payments do not reduce the profits recoverable by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Mason v. Graham and Steam Stone Cutter Co. v. Windsor Mfg. Co.; these payouts are not proper offsets against profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition effects (price reductions increasing plaintiff sales) are relevant to profits question
rubrics_metrics.description: Where competition produced by the infringement increases the plaintiff's sales by reason of reduced prices, this fact is to be considered in assessing profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ingersoll v. Musgrove; the market-wide effects of infringing pricing may affect calculation of gains and losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant must prove affirmative innovations or improvements for deductions
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the defendant claims credits because he used other improvements of his own, he must affirmatively prove those improvements and their effect to obtain deductions from profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as burden of proof on defendant; cases require affirmative proof (American Nicholson Pavement Co. v. City of Elizabeth and others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits on combination patents limited to profits from the exact new features
rubrics_metrics.description: On a patent for a combination, only the profits on the exact new features of the invention can be recovered; the monopoly's profits cannot be arbitrarily divided among parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Ingels v. Mast and related authorities; emphasizes care in apportionment where invention is a combination and the patented elements are a unit.
